artworks.title: Lobby
artworks.description: Here you will check in at the front desk, drop your coats and bags in the coat room or lockers, and grab a map of the museum. Make sure to look up and see the Pteranodon family welcoming you in!

artworks.description: The Extended Lobby displays welcome visitors to the museum and provide an overview of the collections. From here you can start a walk through time in Burke Hall of Dinosaurs, relax in the Central Gallery, or ride the elevator to the galleries on the second and third floors. The Extended Lobby is also the entrance for group visits.

artworks.title: Alison F. Richard Study Gallery
artworks.description: Our experiences with natural history and human culture shape our understanding of the world. The Alison F. Richard Study Gallery offers a unique opportunity for self-directed engagement with both natural and human-made items. Each semester, faculty collaborate with Museum staff to display objects relevant to their courses. This supports the Peabody’s efforts to experiment with curatorial approaches and spark interdisciplinary dialog across the University.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Alison F. Richard Study Gallery
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Basic Drawing
artworks.description: This course serves as an introduction to drawing, emphasizing the use of space and arrangement of visual objects. Sessions are focused on creating drawings based on close observation. Class projects use historical and recent artistic practice as a resource to address challenges in drawing technique.

artworks.galleryName: Alison F. Richard Study Gallery
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Evolutionary Biology
artworks.description: This display explores the importance of forming and testing hypotheses in evolutionary biology through specimens with more complicated evolutionary tales than researchers originally assumed.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Alison F. Richard Study Gallery

artworks.title: Plants and People
artworks.description: This course explores the interaction of plants and people throughout history from biological, historical, anthropological, and artistic perspectives.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum

artworks.title: Vampires, Castles, and Werewolves
artworks.description: Examining gothic novels from the 18th and 19th centuries alongside 20th and 21st-century films, this course explores the historical origins and deep cultural legacy of literary responses to the so-called Age of Reason.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Alison F. Richard Study Gallery

artworks.title: Student Gallery
artworks.description: This space provides a blank canvas for Yale students to explore what museums can be in the 21st century. Here, students share their art, scientific research, and experiences of the natural world and human culture. Peabody Museum staff support students in creating original work, selecting objects from the collections, and designing and building their exhibitions, providing hands-on experience in exhibition design, development, and fabrication.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Student Gallery

artworks.title: Spineless
artworks.description: This exhibition highlights the historical, present, and future applications of invertebrate use and research, particularly as it relates to the advancement of biological science and human health.

artworks.title: Burke Hall: Ancient Oceans
artworks.description: Life first evolved in the oceans. Simple lifeforms, like bacteria and other microbes, have existed for billions of years. Complex life emerged about 600 million years ago. Ancestors of modern animals appeared during the Cambrian Explosion, around 540 million years ago. In its aftermath, marine animals diversified, giving rise to sponges, worms, shrimp-like forms, and fish-like creatures—our own ancestors. Upon entering, you’ll see large ammonites with fascinating preservation. Under the balcony, Peabody research on fossilization and early life shows the oldest life on display in the gallery. The curved blue wall displays some treasures from the Peabody’s invertebrate fossil collections. You’ll see displays of ancient fish, echinoderms, and the Permian Extinction, which nearly destroyed all life on earth.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Burke Hall of Dinosaurs: Life Among Dinosaurs and Ancient Oceans, under The Age of Reptiles mural
artworks.placeNote: Burke Hall, on the museum’s floor plan (Ancient Oceans is part of the hall).

artworks.title: Burke Hall: Life Among Dinosaurs
artworks.description: Welcome to Life among Dinosaurs. In the wake of the extinction event, 252 million years ago, a new fauna emerged. Two large dinosaurs, Brontosaurus and Stegosaurus, occupy the middle of the room. Around the perimeter of the room, you can explore fossil deposits of different ages and locations – including fossils found locally. Under The Age of Reptiles mural by Rudolph Zallinger, we explore the evolution of locomotion through examining fossils. Learn about tetrapods emerging from aquatic to terrestrial environments, the adoption of an upright posture that allowed breathing while running, and the origins of powered flight. You’ll learn that many aspects of locomotion evolved for different purposes and were later used in another way.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Burke Hall of Dinosaurs: Life Among Dinosaurs and Ancient Oceans, under The Age of Reptiles mural
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Ammonites

artworks.title: The Human Footprint
artworks.description: The early evolution and spread of humans around the planet were shaped by their environments. Over time, the effects of human activities have become visible everywhere. Evidence of human interactions with these environments is seen in the record of changes in animal and plant fossils, the chemistry of rocks, and the objects our ancient relatives left behind. In this gallery, you can learn about huge animals that interacted with early humans, track the evolution of our species through replicas of fossilized remains, and understand how humans continue to affect the environment today.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: The Human Footprint
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Moa
artworks.description: Humans reached the islands of New Zealand less than 1,000 years ago. Their activities drove the moa to extinction within only 150 years.

artworks.title: Giant Ground Sloth

artworks.title: A World of Change
artworks.description: A massive asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago and profoundly changed our planet. More than three-quarters of plant and animal species went extinct. When the world finally recovered, the only dinosaurs left were birds. Mammals took over most of the roles dinosaurs once filled. Without that catastrophe, humans wouldn’t be here today. But it also took many other changes to produce the world we now live in. Major shifts in climate, land, and oceans unfolded over tens of millions of years. A warm greenhouse environment, with high levels of gases like carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, became a cooler, drier, icehouse world.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: A World of Change: life after the dinosaurs, the age of mammals
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Gastornis Model

artworks.galleryName: A World of Change: life after the dinosaurs, the age of mammals

artworks.title: Sabelites Frond

artworks.title: Extinct Alligator

artworks.title: Megacerops Skeleton

artworks.title: Menoceras Bone Bed

artworks.title: About Time
artworks.description: We usually measure time with a clock or a calendar. What can we learn about time from fossils, plants, meteorites, and animals? This temporary exhibition dives deep into our collections to show us a clear picture of a moment millions of years ago, and reveals patterns unfolding over centuries. By looking closely, we can unlock information about distant times and places that help us understand our world today.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Special Exhibitions (the temporary gallery)
artworks.placeNote: A temporary show; the museum doesn’t say which room, so placing it in the Special Exhibitions gallery (the second-floor temporary gallery) is our guess.

artworks.title: Unfolding History
artworks.description: May–November 2026 The Yale Peabody Museum’s newest temporary exhibition goes back 4,000 years to explore the origins of writing. Yale researchers are studying a set of tiny document fragments, forgotten since their arrival at the Brooklyn Museum in 1947, to learn more about this crucial moment for human communication – when understanding moved beyond the palace of the pharaoh to the daily lives of regular people.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Special Exhibitions (the temporary gallery)
artworks.placeNote: A temporary show; the museum doesn’t say which room, so placing it in the Special Exhibitions gallery (the second-floor temporary gallery) is our guess.

artworks.title: Soft Traces
artworks.description: Starting July 2026 What kinds of objects or encounters quietly leave traces on us? How do culture and identity continuously shape the body? Inherited knowledge, language, memory, and ancestry are often intangible. Inspired by Taíno body stamps, the artist thought about how temporary identifiers can represent the ways our immaterial cultures are always part of us. Soft Traces proposes that cultural identity persists through embodied experience, repeated gestures, and everyday acts. The artwork fully exists only whea person touches it to create an impression on their skin.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Special Exhibitions (the temporary gallery)
artworks.placeNote: A temporary show; the museum doesn’t say which room, so placing it in the Special Exhibitions gallery (the second-floor temporary gallery) is our guess.

artworks.title: Picturing at the Peabody
artworks.description: Starting May 2026 This exhibition was developed by Yale students in the course “Picturing at the Peabody”. This course, a collaboration between the Yale School of Art and the Peabody Museum, invited students to make photographic work in Peabody spaces, including the galleries, Imaging Studio, and natural properties. At the Peabody and elsewhere, students learned about the history of photography and how the Peabody collections are studied, organized, and exhibited.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Special Exhibitions (the temporary gallery)
artworks.placeNote: A temporary show; the museum doesn’t say which room, so placing it in the Special Exhibitions gallery (the second-floor temporary gallery) is our guess.

artworks.title: The Rocks Cry Out
artworks.description: Starting September 2025 What is the difference between a record and a life? Sculptor Cameron Patricia Downey’s latest work brings together an array of found objects to question how we define who—or what—is a witness. Do these materials’ rich histories, touched by the actions of people or the Earth, imbue them with a kind of life? Inspired by the museum’s collections, Downey created this installation as the Yale Peabody Museum’s 2025 Summer Art Fellow, co-sponsored by the Yale School of Art.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Special Exhibitions (the temporary gallery)
artworks.placeNote: A temporary show; the museum doesn’t say which room, so placing it in the Special Exhibitions gallery (the second-floor temporary gallery) is our guess.

artworks.title: There Are No Horses on Horse Island
artworks.description: Starting April 2025 Here the artist explores the natural landscape and local history of Horse Island through photography and personal reflections. Her black and white images have an ethereal quality, and at first glance the contexts are hard to place. Located in Branford, Connecticut, Horse Island is an environmentally protected area maintained by the Peabody Museum. Voulgaris spent a week there in a residency co-sponsored by the Peabody and the Yale School of Art. This residency is self-directed for an artist who is interested in living and creating while camping in rugged terrain.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Special Exhibitions (the temporary gallery)
artworks.placeNote: A temporary show; the museum doesn’t say which room, so placing it in the Special Exhibitions gallery (the second-floor temporary gallery) is our guess.

artworks.title: History of Science and Technology
artworks.description: The objects in this gallery from the Peabody’s History of Science and Technology Collection shed light on centuries of teaching, research, everyday life, industry, and injustice at Yale and beyond. Most are from Europe and North American in the last 500 years, yet they connect to stories from around the world and across millennia. The intriguing and significant items on display illustrate that science and technology rely on collaborations and exchanges. Countless people – including women and indigenous and enslaved individuals – have contributed to this collective work across time and around the world.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: History of Science and Technology
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Science at Yale
artworks.description: Yale University has a long history of research, education, and innovation – with ties to national and global events, interests, and injustices.

artworks.galleryName: History of Science and Technology

artworks.title: Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia
artworks.description: The people of the ancient Middle East made incredible advances in communication systems, mathematics, and systems of government. Spiritual and religious beliefs played an important role in the day-to-day lives of many. The objects in this gallery relate to lived experiences, from the mundane to the sublime, recording ancient lives. You will learn about ongoing Yale research and find connections between these ancient civilizations and the region today.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia (funerary items on display)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: The World’s Oldest Written Recipes
artworks.description: These 4,000-year-old cuneiform tablets are the earliest written recipes. They include stews, pies, and some foreign dishes, revealing culinary sophistication in ancient Mesopotamia.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia (funerary items on display)

artworks.title: Writing in Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia
artworks.description: Sumerian cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs emerged around the same time in the late 4th millennium BCE. The two cultures initially used writing for different purposes.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia (funerary items on display)

artworks.title: Math Through the Millennia: The Square Root of 2

artworks.title: Mesoamerican and Andean Civilizations
artworks.description: This gallery shows the parallel development of civilizations in Mesoamerica and the Andes. Through millennia the Indigenous peoples of these regions developed diverse cultures and domesticated animals and plants—including the corn and potatoes that feed billions of people today. Pottery, textiles, sculptures, instruments, and other materials on view span 3,000 years of history. They illustrate a range of complex stories, including writing, music, animal husbandry, architecture, religion, ritual, and trade.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Mesoamerican and Andean Civilizations (funerary items on display)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Feather Textile
artworks.description: This textile, made of parrot feathers from the Amazon rainforest and cotton from the coast of Peru, shows the range of the Huari empire.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Mesoamerican and Andean Civilizations (funerary items on display)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Lambayeque Whistling Bottle
artworks.description: Chambered bottles like this one often had whistles added to them. The whistle would make distinctive sounds as corn beer was poured from the vessel.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Mesoamerican and Andean Civilizations (funerary items on display)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Olmec Head – Replica
artworks.description: Monumental architecture and sculpture in Mesoamerica began with the Olmec civilization. This is a replica of an enormous sculpture, likely a portrait of a ruler.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Mesoamerican and Andean Civilizations (funerary items on display)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Hall of the Pacific
artworks.description: The new Hall of the Pacific is the Peabody’s first permanent display of the traditional arts and cultural objects of the region. Over 250 items on display are sculptures and textiles from the collection of Thomas Jaffe ‘71 as well as those from the Museum’s collection. The gallery features small personal ornaments, functional objects such as canoe paddles, drums, shields made for protection, vessels, examples of masks made throughout the region, a painted house façade, barkcloth, and figurative sculptures made from materials found in the region. Click ‘Read More’ to view additional text information from inside the Hall of the Pacific gallery, made accessible via QR codes.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Hall of the Pacific
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Tago Mask
artworks.description: Tago appeared in Tami Island villages once in a decade representing mythical ancestors or spirits. Tago, owned by clans, are made by men in secret.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Tom Jaffe / Johan Vipper
artworks.galleryName: Hall of the Pacific
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Pair of Eharo Masks
artworks.description: The Elema people of the Papuan Gulf performed a masking cycle during important events. Eharo sculptural elements represent totemic animals, birds, fish, or reptiles.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Tom Jaffe / Johan Vipper
artworks.galleryName: Hall of the Pacific
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: The Island of New Guinea
artworks.description: The Island of New Guinea has over 800 languages. It is divided politically; Indonesia in the west and independent Papua New Guinea in the east.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Tom Jaffe / Johan Vipper
artworks.galleryName: Hall of the Pacific
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Prestige and Ceremony in Fiji
artworks.description: Fijian artists make sculptures and textiles reflecting many aspects of their culture. During ceremonies men of status display specific objects. Women make masi (barkcloth).
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Tom Jaffe / Johan Vipper
artworks.galleryName: Hall of the Pacific
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Malangan Ritual Art
artworks.description: Over a long period of time the people of New Ireland developed an extensive art tradition used in a sacred ritual context.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Tom Jaffe / Johan Vipper
artworks.galleryName: Hall of the Pacific
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Minerals, Earth and Space
artworks.description: Earth formed as part of our solar system more than 4.5 billion years ago. It has been shaped by powerful geologic forces over its entire history and will continue to change for billions of years to come. Societies depend on Earth’s vast mineral and energy resources and on a climate that allows life to flourish. In the Mineral Galleries at the Peabody, you can learn more about the Solar System, how minerals are formed, gems and jewelry, and the history of mineralogy at Yale. David Friend Hall, the largest gallery, features artistic presentations of remarkable minerals from around the world.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: David Friend Hall: minerals and gems (Minerals, Earth and Space)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Quartz Sandstone Concretion
artworks.description: The undulating shape of sandstone concretions in the Fontainebleau quartz sand deposits southeast of Paris, France have for centuries fascinated humans.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: David Friend Hall: minerals and gems (Minerals, Earth and Space)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: “The Rocket”
artworks.description: At 3.5 feet (107 centimeters) and 300 pounds (136 kilograms), this tourmaline-group mineral is the largest and most spectacular found in Brazil’s Bambúrro mineral pocket. On loan from the Yampol Family and The Mineral Trust.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: David Friend Hall: minerals and gems (Minerals, Earth and Space)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Fulgurite
artworks.description: This 13-foot (4-meter) sand tube formed in an instant when lightning struck Miller’s Beach on Congamond Lakes in Connecticut in 1949.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: David Friend Hall: minerals and gems (Minerals, Earth and Space)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Fluorescent Minerals
artworks.description: These mineral specimens erupt in a riot of color when exposed to ultraviolet (aka black) “light.”
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Harold Moritz
artworks.galleryName: David Friend Hall: minerals and gems (Minerals, Earth and Space)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Cora Miller Bequest Case
artworks.description: The array of semiprecious and precious stones in the Cora Miller Bequest Case displays a spectrum of colors from purple quartz (amethyst) to fiery opal.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: David Friend Hall: minerals and gems (Minerals, Earth and Space)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: North American Dioramas
artworks.description: Variation in geology and climate helps drive and maintain biological diversity. Because temperature, moisture, and light levels vary with latitude and longitude, elevation, and soil type, animals and plants have evolved physical and behavioral adaptations suited to the environments created by these conditions. North America is home to many tens of thousands of animal and plant species, many of which are closely tied to specific ecological communities. These communities range from treeless Arctic tundra to lush tropical rainforests.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: North American Dioramas
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Tropical Rainforest
artworks.description: North American tropical rainforests are found in the southernmost areas of the continent and are among its most species-rich regions.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: North American Dioramas
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: High Arctic Tundra
artworks.description: This habitat is one of the most northern points of land on Earth. Though growing conditions are harsh, many dozens of species occur here.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: North American Dioramas
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Sonoran Desert
artworks.description: The Sonoran Desert spans southeastern California and northwestern Mexico. Because it gets very little rain, species have adaptated to the hot, dry conditions.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: North American Dioramas
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Dynamic Nature
artworks.description: Earth is home to millions of recognized species, with more being found every day. They exhibit an incredible range of forms, functions, behaviors, life histories, and interactions. After years of study and observation, Charles Darwin provided substantial evidence for evolution, along with a mechanism—natural selection—for how it happens. Support for evolution is widespread. It is found in many places: the fossil record, genetics, the form and structure of organisms, and where they live on the planet.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Dynamic Nature
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: A Close Fit
artworks.description: Evolution can lead to specialized relationships among living things. Some species of columbine have flowers that have evolved to fit the mouth of a moth.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Dynamic Nature
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Look-Alikes
artworks.description: Evolution can lead to similarities between unrelated organisms. Mammals have independently evolved spines four times, likely as a defense against predators.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Dynamic Nature
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Deceptive Forms
artworks.description: Many species have evolved deceptive color patterns, shapes, smells, and behaviors. The mantis shrimp has threatening eyespots on its tail and shell, to frighten predators.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Dynamic Nature
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Use it or Lose It
artworks.description: Over time, some features of living things—like wings—may be reduced, lost, or repurposed. Kiwis and cassowaries have each lost the ability to fly.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Dynamic Nature
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Radical Change
artworks.description: Many organisms take on different forms during their lifetimes. Caterpillars—juvenile stages of moths and butterflies—eat plant parts while adults drink nectar or sap.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Dynamic Nature
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Connecticut Dioramas
artworks.description: The many habitats in New England are typical of North America. They influence the distribution of biodiversity over space and time. Our area was covered by glaciers as recently as 20,000 years ago. As the climate warmed the glaciers retreated. Plants and animals migrated to fill the landscape. The dioramas in this hall feature three biological communities that one might encounter in Connecticut. Created over 70 years ago, the scenes were modeled on real locations within the state. Since their creation, many environmental changes have occurred in the region, including climate change, overdevelopment, and the spread of non-native invasive plants.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Connecticut Dioramas
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Coastal Region
artworks.description: This diorama is modeled after Milford Point. It features a beach, a salt marsh that extends inland along a river, and a nearby farm.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Connecticut Dioramas
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Forest Margin
artworks.description: This diorama depicts a deciduous forest in late summer in Litchfield County. It features a variety of native forest species; invasive plants are not shown.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Connecticut Dioramas
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Cold Bog
artworks.description: This bog is located in Connecticut’s Great Mountain Forest in Litchfield County. The black spruces found here are more common farther north.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Connecticut Dioramas
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Living Lab
artworks.description: The Living Lab is home to live animals, including butterflies, poison dart frogs, lizards, and an eastern indigo snake. This gallery displays an array of objects from across the museum’s collections. Most of the Peabody’s galleries feature items selected by curators to tell a story. In the Living Lab, visitors are invited to explore and form their own stories based on what they see.
artworks.imageCredit: Yale Peabody Museum (peabody.yale.edu)
artworks.galleryName: Living Lab: live animals and things you can touch
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Turtles
artworks.description: We’re used to seeing turtles from the back and sides. In the Living Lab, we’ve flipped our turtles onto their backs for a different view.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Living Lab: live animals and things you can touch
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: How Many Shades of Blue?
artworks.description: These are just some of the many varieties of blue in nature. But how is the color blue made? In different ways, it turns out.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Living Lab: live animals and things you can touch
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: Poison Dart Frogs
artworks.description: These colorful critters are native to tropical Central and South America. How many different species can you spot?
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Living Lab: live animals and things you can touch
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.

artworks.title: North American Freshwater Stream Fishes
artworks.description: The freshwater streams and rivers of the eastern United States host the highest fish diversity of any non-tropical freshwater habitat.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Andy Melien / Yale Peabody Museum
artworks.galleryName: Living Lab: live animals and things you can touch
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor plan and gallery page put it.
